  • Anti-Censorship/Accountability of Private Power: Proponents worry about the power of large tech platforms to unilaterally decide what speech is acceptable. Mandating platforms to host all legal content avoids the pitfalls of attempting to define and regulate such a subjective category.
  • Streisand Effect: Attempting to suppress or censor content, even hateful content, can sometimes backfire and draw more attention to it. The censorship itself becomes the story, and the suppressed content gains notoriety. A more open approach, where problematic content is allowed but vigorously challenged, can be more effective in the long run.

  • Bad ideas should be debunked through speech, not suppression. The best way to combat harmful or offensive speech (e.g., hate speech) is to counter it with better arguments, not to remove it. Removing speech denies society the chance to address it directly.

4. Avoiding a Slippery Slope of Censorship

Critics fear that without clear legal limits, platform censorship will expand beyond its original intent:

  • Creators retain control: Artists, journalists, and activists would not risk losing their entire audience or income streams due to a single post or a platform’s opaque moderation decisions.
  • Reduced moderation costs: Platforms spend vast resources on moderation teams and AI systems to enforce policies. A legal mandate could simplify this by reducing the scope of what needs moderation (i.e., only illegal content).

  1. Platforms are private entities with their own rights: They have the right to curate their spaces, just as a newspaper chooses its editorial stance. Compelling them to host all legal content could violate their free speech rights.

The arguments for such a mandate are rooted in:

  3. Preserve a robust marketplace of ideas where harmful speech is countered by better arguments, not suppressed.

The Case for Mandatory Hosting: Why Social Media Platforms Should Be Treated as Common Carriers

Introduction

The modern public square is no longer the town plaza or the newspaper editorial page. It is Twitter/X, Facebook, YouTube, Reddit, and a handful of other platforms that collectively serve as the infrastructure through which billions of people communicate, organize, and express themselves. This tectonic shift in how speech occurs raises a question that liberal democracies can no longer afford to leave unresolved: should private corporations have unchecked editorial discretion over the speech of billions?

This essay argues that major social media platforms and online services should be legally required to host all lawful content—including content from hate groups, political extremists, and other deeply objectionable voices—and should be classified as common carriers subject to nondiscrimination obligations. This position rests not on sympathy for hateful ideas but on a principled commitment to free expression, structural accountability, and the preservation of democratic self-governance in the digital age.

I. The Structural Reality: Platforms as Infrastructure

The common carrier doctrine has deep roots in Anglo-American law. Railroads, telegraph companies, telephone networks, and broadband providers have all been subject to nondiscrimination obligations because they control essential infrastructure and exercise gatekeeper power over public communication. The logic is straightforward: when a private entity becomes so central to public life that exclusion from its services effectively silences a speaker, that entity ceases to be a mere private publisher and becomes something more akin to a public utility.

Social media platforms now occupy precisely this structural position. For billions of users worldwide—and for an overwhelming majority in many countries—platforms like Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok are the internet. They are where political organizing happens, where small businesses reach customers, where journalists distribute reporting, and where ordinary citizens participate in public discourse. When a platform bans a user or removes content, it does not merely exercise editorial discretion the way a newspaper choosing not to publish a letter to the editor does. It exercises a form of privatized censorship with consequences that can be functionally equivalent to government suppression.

The scale of these platforms has no historical precedent. Facebook alone has roughly three billion monthly active users. No newspaper, broadcast network, or public forum has ever wielded comparable communicative power. Treating entities of this magnitude as ordinary private publishers engaged in "editorial judgment" is a legal fiction that fails to account for structural reality.

Telecommunications companies like AT&T carry billions of conversations every day. We do not permit them to disconnect a customer because they disapprove of the customer's political views. We recognize that AT&T's infrastructure role imposes special obligations. Social media platforms, which now carry orders of magnitude more public discourse than any telecommunications company, deserve no less scrutiny—and no fewer obligations.

II. The Free Speech Principle: Protecting the Speech We Hate

The philosophical case for protecting hateful speech is not new. It is, in fact, the foundational insight of the free speech tradition itself. As Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote in United States v. Schwimmer (1929), "If there is any principle of the Constitution that more imperatively calls for attachment than any other, it is the principle of free thought—not free thought for those who agree with us but freedom for the thought that we hate."

This principle exists precisely because the value of free speech is not contingent on the content of the speech. If we protect only popular or agreeable speech, we protect nothing at all, because popular speech needs no protection. The entire apparatus of free expression exists to shield the unpopular, the offensive, and the transgressive from suppression by those who hold power—including the power of social approval.

When we argue that platforms should be permitted to remove hate speech, we are arguing, in substance, that a small number of Silicon Valley executives and content moderation teams should have the power to determine which ideas are too dangerous for billions of people to encounter. This is a staggering delegation of quasi-governmental authority to unaccountable private actors. It presupposes that these actors will exercise this power wisely, consistently, and in the public interest—assumptions for which there is little evidence and considerable contrary evidence.

Content moderation at scale is notoriously inconsistent, opaque, and error-prone. Platforms have suppressed Palestinian advocacy, Black Lives Matter content, legitimate journalism about war crimes, and political speech from across the ideological spectrum—all in the name of fighting "harmful" content. The category of "hate speech" itself is notoriously difficult to define with precision. What one moderator considers hate speech, another may consider legitimate political commentary. Entire academic fields cannot agree on where protected criticism of ideas ends and unprotected hatred of persons begins. Entrusting this inherently subjective determination to corporate employees operating under commercial incentives is not a solution to the problem of harmful speech—it is merely the substitution of one form of arbitrary power for another.

The strongest free speech regimes have always operated on the principle that the remedy for harmful speech is more speech, not enforced silence. When we ban hateful ideas from public platforms, we do not eliminate those ideas. We drive them underground, where they fester without challenge, where adherents find solidarity without exposure to counter-arguments, and where radicalization accelerates in echo chambers rather than being tempered by public contestation. The marketplace of ideas is not a quaint metaphor—it is a functional mechanism by which bad ideas are exposed, challenged, and ultimately defeated. But the marketplace cannot function if powerful intermediaries preemptively remove ideas from the exchange.

III. The Democratic Argument: No Private Veto on Public Discourse

Democracy requires that citizens be able to freely discuss, debate, and deliberate on matters of public concern—including matters that some citizens find deeply offensive. The question of immigration, of racial identity, of religious doctrine, of cultural change—these are legitimate topics of democratic debate, and citizens on all sides of these debates sometimes express themselves in ways that others find hateful. If platforms are empowered to suppress one side of these debates under the label of "hate speech," they exercise a de facto veto on democratic deliberation.

Consider the practical consequences. In the United States, political parties, advocacy organizations, and individual citizens rely on social media to organize, fundraise, and communicate with supporters. When platforms selectively enforce content policies against disfavored political viewpoints—and the evidence strongly suggests that enforcement patterns track the political preferences of platform leadership and employees—they distort the democratic process. This is true whether the enforcement targets the left or the right, whether it suppresses radical voices or merely controversial ones.

The answer is not government control of platforms—that would create its own dangers. The answer is a legal framework that removes the platform's editorial discretion over lawful content, just as we removed telecommunications companies' discretion over who could use the telephone network. Common carrier regulation does not require the government to dictate what platforms carry. It simply requires platforms to carry all lawful content on equal terms, removing their power to discriminate based on viewpoint.

IV. Addressing the Counterarguments

"Platforms are private companies with First Amendment rights."

This argument conflates two distinct questions. The First Amendment, as currently interpreted, restricts only government action. But the policy question of whether platforms should be required to host lawful content is separate from the constitutional question of whether the First Amendment mandates it. Common carrier obligations can be—and historically have been—imposed on private entities by statute. The Telecommunications Act of 1934, the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and numerous state public accommodation laws all restrict the "editorial discretion" of private businesses in service of overriding public interests. The question is whether the public interest in open discourse justifies similar obligations for dominant platforms, and the structural analysis above suggests that it does.

Moreover, the Supreme Court's decision in Packingham v. North Carolina (2017) recognized that social media platforms are "the modern public square," strongly suggesting that the Court perceives a public interest dimension to platform access that transcends mere private property rights. Lower courts and legislatures are increasingly grappling with this tension, and the trajectory of the law is moving—slowly but unmistakably—toward recognizing that dominant platforms occupy a special position that warrants regulatory obligations.

"Hosting hate speech causes real harm to marginalized communities."

This is the strongest counterargument, and it deserves a serious response. Hate speech can indeed cause psychological harm, contribute to hostile environments, and—when it crosses into incitement—lead to real-world violence. None of this should be minimized.

However, the solution to harmful speech cannot be to grant private corporations the power to determine which speech is too harmful to be permitted in the public square. This power is too great, too easily abused, and too poorly exercised to be left in corporate hands. The legal system already provides tools for addressing speech that constitutes true threats, incitement to imminent lawless action, harassment, or defamation. These are narrow, well-defined categories with established legal standards. A common carrier obligation would not require platforms to host speech that is illegal—only speech that is lawful but offensive. The distinction matters.

Furthermore, the history of censorship teaches us that the power to suppress "harmful" speech invariably falls hardest on the marginalized communities it purports to protect. LGBTQ+ content has been repeatedly flagged as "sexual" or "inappropriate" by platform moderation systems. Sex workers, drug reform advocates, and harm reduction organizations have seen their content suppressed under "community standards" that were ostensibly designed to protect vulnerable users. Those with the least social power are consistently the least able to navigate or challenge opaque corporate censorship regimes. A rule of clear, law-based content standards—rather than discretionary corporate judgment—serves the interests of marginalized communities more reliably than the current system.

"Platforms would be overrun with extremist content."

This argument assumes that the current volume of extremist content on platforms is kept manageable only by active moderation. But several facts complicate this assumption. First, platforms already host enormous quantities of extremist, hateful, and offensive content, and their moderation systems demonstrably fail to remove more than a fraction of it. Second, algorithmic amplification—rather than mere hosting—is the primary mechanism by which extremist content spreads. A common carrier obligation need not prevent platforms from adjusting recommendation algorithms to avoid amplifying harmful content; it would simply require them to host lawful content without discrimination. Third, platforms like 4chan, which have minimal content moderation, have not collapsed into unusability—they have developed community norms, user-driven moderation, and other informal mechanisms for managing discourse.

The distinction between hosting and amplification is critical and is often elided in this debate. Requiring platforms to carry lawful content does not require them to promote it, recommend it, or amplify it. It simply requires them not to remove it.

V. A Workable Framework

A common carrier obligation for major social media platforms would include the following elements:

Free speech is not a gift that the powerful extend to the powerless. In the digital age, structural protection requires treating the dominant platforms as what they are: the essential infrastructure of public discourse, subject to obligations commensurate with their power.

The Case for Mandatory Content Neutrality: Why Online Platforms Should Host All Legal Speech

The digital public square has become the primary venue for political debate, community organization, and information exchange in the twenty-first century. Yet this essential infrastructure remains under the arbitrary control of a handful of private corporations whose moderation decisions increasingly shape the boundaries of acceptable discourse. The time has come to recognize that dominant social media platforms and online services function as the modern equivalent of telephone networks and railways, and should be legally required to host all constitutionally protected speech—including speech from groups whose views we find repugnant. This obligation flows naturally from both absolute free speech principles and the longstanding common carrier tradition in American law.

The Common Carrier Tradition Applies to Digital Infrastructure

Common carrier doctrine emerged from a simple recognition: when certain businesses become essential conduits for commerce and communication, they acquire obligations beyond those of ordinary private enterprises. Railroads cannot refuse passengers based on their political views. Telephone companies cannot disconnect customers for the content of their conversations. Electric utilities cannot cut power to households whose residents espouse unpopular ideas. The underlying principle is that when a service becomes sufficiently essential to participation in economic and civic life, the operator's private property rights must yield to the public's interest in non-discriminatory access.

Major social media platforms meet every traditional criterion for common carrier status. They hold themselves out to serve the general public. They have achieved network effects that make them functionally unavoidable for modern political participation—a politician, activist, or journalist excluded from major platforms suffers a profound disadvantage that cannot be remedied by migrating to competitors. Justice Clarence Thomas recognized this reality in his 2021 concurrence in Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute, observing that the concentration of digital power in a few platforms presents precisely the conditions under which common carrier obligations have historically been imposed.

The fact that these platforms are privately owned is not a conclusive objection. Private railroads, private telegraph companies, and private telephone providers have all been subjected to carriage obligations. The relevant question is not ownership but function: does the service constitute essential infrastructure for public life? For Facebook, YouTube, and X, the answer is plainly yes.

Free Speech Requires Protecting Speech We Hate

The principle that free expression must extend to hateful speech is not a concession to bigotry but the foundation of any genuinely free society. The First Amendment's protection of Nazi marchers in Skokie, of Klan rallies, and of the Westboro Baptist Church's funeral protests rests on a hard-won insight: once the state or any powerful institution is empowered to silence disfavored viewpoints, that power will inevitably expand and be turned against whoever currently lacks influence. The history of censorship is the history of majorities suppressing minorities, of the powerful silencing the powerless, of orthodoxies protecting themselves from challenge.

Critics respond that private platforms are not the state and therefore are not bound by First Amendment principles. This is technically correct but substantively inadequate. When private entities exercise state-like power over the conditions of public discourse, the values animating the First Amendment apply with similar urgency. A regime in which the government cannot censor but a handful of tech executives can exile anyone from the effective public square delivers only a hollow version of free expression.

Moreover, platform moderation of legal speech has repeatedly proven to be both arbitrary and politically lopsided. Categories like "misinformation" and "hate speech" lack stable definitions and have been used to suppress speech that was later vindicated, including early discussion of the Hunter Biden laptop story and certain hypotheses about the origins of COVID-19. When the criteria for exclusion are elastic enough to capture mainstream political speech, the case for trusting platforms with discretionary power over public discourse collapses.

The Counterproductive Nature of Deplatforming

Deplatforming hate groups does not eliminate their ideas; it disperses them into less visible, more radical corners of the internet where they can incubate without challenge. Sunlight remains the best disinfectant. Bad ideas are most effectively defeated when exposed to public refutation, not driven underground where their adherents develop siege mentalities and recruit in echo chambers. The civil rights movement, the gay rights movement, and countless other causes that were once considered dangerous or obscene triumphed precisely because free speech protections allowed them to be heard. A regime of content moderation calibrated to the sensibilities of the current moment would have suppressed many of these movements in their early days.

Hosting speech is not endorsing it. The telephone company does not endorse every conversation carried over its wires. Requiring platforms to carry lawful speech would not implicate them in that speech any more than requiring a bus company to transport all paying passengers implicates it in their views.

A Workable Legal Framework

Implementing mandatory content neutrality does not require accepting chaos. A sensible framework would apply carriage obligations only to platforms exceeding a certain size threshold, preserving space for smaller curated communities. It would require hosting of all legal speech while permitting time, place, and manner restrictions—including user-controlled filtering tools that let individuals curate their own experience without platforms imposing top-down editorial control. It would allow platforms to label, contextualize, or deprioritize content without removing it. Illegal speech—true threats, incitement, child exploitation—would remain unprotected, as it is under existing First Amendment doctrine.

This approach respects both the reality that platforms must make some operational decisions and the principle that they should not function as ideological gatekeepers. It also empowers users rather than paternalistically protecting them, trusting adults to decide what they wish to see.

Conclusion

The question is not whether we find certain views detestable—many of us do—but who should decide what speech reaches the public. The answer cannot be a handful of unaccountable corporate executives operating under opaque and shifting standards. Dominant online platforms have become the essential infrastructure of modern public life, and they should bear the same obligation of non-discriminatory service that we have long imposed on other essential carriers. Protecting even hateful speech is the price of maintaining a society in which unpopular truths can eventually prevail over comfortable lies. This price has always been worth paying, and the emergence of digital public squares does not change that calculus—it only raises the stakes.

Digital Platforms as Modern Public Squares: The Case for Content-Neutral Hosting Requirements

In the 21st century, social media platforms and online services have become the primary venues for public discourse, effectively replacing traditional town squares and public forums. These digital spaces now host the conversations that shape our democracy, culture, and society. Given their fundamental role in facilitating speech and communication, these platforms should be legally required to host all lawful content without discrimination, operating under common carrier principles that have long governed essential communication services.

The Common Carrier Precedent

Telephone companies cannot disconnect your service because they disagree with your conversations. The postal service cannot refuse to deliver your mail based on its content. These entities operate as common carriers—neutral conduits for communication that must serve all users equally. The principle is simple: when a service becomes essential infrastructure for public communication, it forfeits the right to discriminate based on content.

Today's dominant platforms—Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, and others—have achieved a similar status. They are no longer mere private companies but essential infrastructure for modern communication. When a handful of corporations control the primary means of public discourse, they wield unprecedented power over what ideas can be expressed and heard. This concentration of power demands a corresponding obligation to remain neutral.

The Sovereignty of Law

The proposed requirement is not unlimited—platforms would still remove genuinely illegal content such as child exploitation material, true threats, or criminal conspiracy. The key principle is that private corporations should not position themselves as arbiters of acceptable speech beyond what democratic societies have already codified in law. If speech is legal, it should be permitted.

This approach respects the democratic process. Societies have developed legal frameworks through centuries of debate, litigation, and legislation to define the boundaries of acceptable speech. These boundaries, while imperfect, represent collective democratic judgment. When platforms impose additional restrictions, they substitute corporate judgment for democratic decision-making, effectively creating a parallel system of speech governance without democratic accountability.

The Danger of Viewpoint Discrimination

History teaches us that censorship powers, once established, inevitably expand beyond their original intent. Today's "hate speech" policies might target genuinely abhorrent content, but tomorrow they could silence political dissent, unpopular minorities, or challenging ideas. The definition of "harmful" speech shifts with political winds and cultural moments.

Consider how concepts of acceptable speech have evolved. Many ideas now considered mainstream were once deemed dangerous or offensive. Civil rights advocates were once labeled as dangerous radicals. Early feminists were considered threats to social order. LGBTQ+ rights activists faced systematic censorship. Under a regime of corporate speech control, these movements might never have gained the platform necessary to change hearts and minds.

The Marketplace of Ideas in the Digital Age

Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. articulated the concept of the "marketplace of ideas"—that truth emerges through competition between ideas rather than through suppression. This principle becomes even more critical in the digital age, where information moves at unprecedented speed and scale. The answer to bad speech is more speech, not enforced silence.

When platforms remove legal but offensive content, they don't eliminate the underlying ideas—they drive them underground into echo chambers where they fester without challenge. Forcing all legal content onto mainstream platforms ensures that bad ideas face public scrutiny and counter-argument. Sunlight remains the best disinfectant.

Protecting Vulnerable Voices

Paradoxically, strong free speech protections often best serve marginalized communities. Content moderation systems, despite good intentions, frequently silence minority voices through algorithmic bias, cultural misunderstanding, or majoritarian pressure. Automated systems struggle with context, irony, and cultural nuance. Human moderators bring their own biases and cultural blind spots.

A content-neutral hosting requirement protects unpopular minorities from majoritarian censorship. It ensures that dissidents, activists, and cultural outsiders cannot be silenced simply because their views make others uncomfortable. The same principle that protects offensive speech also protects revolutionary speech, minority languages, and subcultural expression.

Democratic Accountability

The current system allows unelected tech executives to make decisions affecting billions of users' ability to speak and hear. These decisions happen behind closed doors, guided by opaque algorithms and inconsistent enforcement. Users have little recourse when wrongly silenced, and there's no democratic input into policy formation.

Requiring platforms to host all legal content returns speech governance to democratic institutions. If society decides certain speech should be prohibited, it can do so through the legislative process, with all the deliberation, accountability, and constitutional constraints that entails. This approach ensures that speech restrictions reflect genuine societal consensus rather than corporate preferences.

Addressing Counter-Arguments

Critics argue that forcing platforms to host offensive content violates their own free speech rights or property rights. However, when platforms achieve monopolistic or oligopolistic control over essential communication infrastructure, traditional property rights must yield to public necessity. We don't allow electric companies to cut power to homes based on residents' political views, despite their private ownership.

Others worry about user experience and platform toxicity. But platforms would retain vast powers to shape user experience through algorithmic recommendation, user blocking tools, and optional filtering systems. The requirement is to host content, not to promote it. Users could still choose what they see while preserving everyone's ability to speak.

Conclusion

The digital public square is too important to be governed by the whims of private corporations. As social media platforms and online services have become essential infrastructure for democratic discourse, they must accept the responsibilities that come with that status. Requiring these platforms to host all legal content respects democratic sovereignty, protects minority voices, and preserves the marketplace of ideas for the digital age.

This is not a radical proposal but a return to principles that have long governed essential communication services. In an era where a few platforms mediate much of human communication, we cannot afford to let private corporations decide which legal ideas may be expressed. The preservation of free speech in the digital age demands nothing less than content-neutral platform obligations. Only by ensuring that all legal voices can be heard can we maintain the robust, chaotic, and vital public discourse that democracy requires.

The Case for Absolute Free Speech and Common Carrier Obligations: Why Social Media Must Host All Legal Content

In an era where digital platforms dominate public discourse, the question of whether social media companies should be legally obligated to host all legal content—including speech from hate groups—has become increasingly contentious. Proponents of strict content moderation argue that platforms must actively suppress harmful speech to protect users and society. However, this position undermines fundamental principles of free speech, common carrier obligations, and the democratic ideal of an open marketplace of ideas. Instead, social media platforms should be legally required to host all constitutionally protected speech, treating them as common carriers rather than private publishers. Only by enforcing absolute free speech principles and common carrier obligations can we preserve the integrity of free expression in the digital age.

1. The First Amendment and Absolute Free Speech

The First Amendment to the United States Constitution establishes that "Congress shall make no law… abridging the freedom of speech." This provision is not merely a historical relic but a foundational guarantee of democratic self-governance. Free speech allows for the exchange of ideas, the exposure of truth, and the correction of error—even from those with whom we disagree. As Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. famously wrote in Schenck v. United States, "The most stringent protection of free speech would not protect a man in falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic." However, this principle does not extend to suppressing speech simply because it is offensive, unpopular, or morally repugnant.

Social media platforms, by their nature, are public forums where individuals and groups engage in discourse. When these platforms selectively censor speech—even legal content—they act as arbiters of truth, a role that belongs to society, not private corporations. If a platform can unilaterally decide what constitutes "hate speech," it sets a dangerous precedent where government or corporate elites determine which ideas are permissible. This is not free speech; it is censorship by proxy.

2. Common Carrier Obligations: The Historical Precedent

The concept of a "common carrier" is a legal doctrine that requires certain businesses—such as telephone companies and railroads—to provide service to all comers without discrimination. This principle ensures that essential services remain neutral and accessible to everyone, preventing monopolistic control over information flow.

Social media platforms, particularly those with near-monopolistic dominance (e.g., Facebook, Twitter/X, YouTube), function as modern-day common carriers. They are not merely publishers but the primary means through which millions communicate, organize, and disseminate ideas. If a telephone company could refuse service to a caller simply because they were discussing a controversial topic, it would be an unconstitutional violation of free expression. The same logic applies to digital platforms.

By enforcing common carrier obligations, we ensure that no single entity—whether a corporation or government—can act as a gatekeeper of speech. This prevents the suppression of marginalized voices, conspiracy theories, or unpopular but legal ideas, which may later be vindicated by public discourse.

3. The Dangers of Platform Censorship

When social media platforms engage in selective censorship, they do not merely moderate content—they shape public opinion. Studies have shown that algorithmic suppression of certain viewpoints can amplify polarization by creating echo chambers where dissenting opinions are systematically excluded. For example, the banning of accounts associated with the QAnon movement or far-right groups may silence legitimate grievances that could be addressed through reasoned debate rather than outright prohibition.

Moreover, private censorship undermines democratic accountability. If a platform can decide which ideas are "acceptable," it introduces an arbitrary standard that is not subject to judicial review. This is particularly problematic when platforms act as de facto censors for governments or activist groups, suppressing speech that might challenge established narratives.

4. The Marketplace of Ideas and the Correction of Error

John Stuart Mill’s On Liberty argues that the best way to combat false or harmful ideas is through open debate, not suppression. If a hate group’s speech is illegal (e.g., incitement to violence), it can be prosecuted under existing laws. But if it is merely offensive or unpopular, silencing it does not eliminate the ideas—it only pushes them underground, where they may fester unchecked.

By contrast, an open platform allows society to engage with problematic ideas, exposing their flaws through reasoned argument. History shows that many once-reviled ideas—from civil rights activism to scientific dissent—were initially met with hostility before gaining mainstream acceptance. Without the ability to express and debate such ideas, progress stalls.

5. Legal and Ethical Obligations of Platforms

If social media platforms are to be held to common carrier standards, they must be treated as neutral conduits rather than editorial decision-makers. This would require:

  • Neutral Moderation Policies: Platforms would be prohibited from banning or deplatforming users based on viewpoint discrimination, only removing content that violates clear legal standards (e.g., incitement to violence, defamation, or illegal activity).
  • Transparency in Algorithms: Users should have the right to appeal content removals and understand how algorithms prioritize or suppress speech.
  • Legal Protections for Users: Individuals should not be liable for legal but controversial speech posted on these platforms, as they would be protected under common carrier immunity.

Conclusion: Free Speech as the Foundation of Democracy

The argument for legally requiring social media platforms to host all legal content is not about endorsing hate or suppressing dissent—it is about preserving the fundamental right to free expression. In a democracy, the marketplace of ideas must remain open, even to those with whom we disagree. Common carrier obligations ensure that no single entity, whether corporate or governmental, can act as an arbiter of truth.

If we abandon this principle, we risk creating a digital world where only the approved narratives are heard, where marginalized voices are silenced, and where the very fabric of democratic discourse is weakened. The alternative—private censorship—is not freedom; it is tyranny by algorithm. The law must enforce absolute free speech and common carrier obligations to ensure that social media remains a space for all legal ideas, not just those deemed palatable by a handful of corporate gatekeepers.

A democracy that fears lawful speech has already dimmed its own lights. In the networked era, social media platforms and major online services function as the streets, newspapers, and telephone lines of public life. When a few companies control the gateways through which most people speak and hear, private moderation becomes public power. To preserve a culture of liberty, the law should require these platforms to host all legal content, including expression from groups most people loathe, while empowering users—not corporations—to choose what they see. This approach explains itself: if speech is lawful, it should be allowed; if it is unlawful, the state must say so clearly and narrowly. Between those poles, neutrality is the only rule compatible with absolute free speech principles and the traditional logic of common carriers.

The philosophical case is straightforward. Free speech is not a prize for the virtuous but a shield for everyone, especially for those out of favor. History shows that speech taboos shift with political winds; yesterday’s heretic becomes tomorrow’s majority, and vice versa. The only stable rule is content neutrality anchored to legality. In the American tradition, the First Amendment enshrines this insight by sharply limiting the government’s power to criminalize speech, carving out narrow categories such as true threats, incitement, defamation, obscenity, and a few others. Hate speech, as such, is legal in the United States. That is not an endorsement of its content; it is a recognition that once a government or a proxy can punish ideas for being hateful, it can punish any disfavored idea. Requiring platforms to host all legal content extends this same principle to private gatekeepers who now wield state-scale influence over public discourse.

Common carrier obligations provide the right legal architecture. For centuries, carriers that “hold themselves out” to the public—railroads, telegraphs, telephones—have been required to carry without discrimination, subject to reasonable terms and safety rules. The justification is not that carriers lack property rights or expression; it is that they possess bottleneck control over essential channels of commerce and communication. Social media and dominant online services now occupy a comparable role. Network effects and switching costs make exit illusory for many users; a platform’s moderation choices become, in practice, speech rules for society. Nondiscriminatory carriage solves this power problem while preserving innovation: platforms can design features, improve security, fight spam, and compete on user experience, but they cannot block lawful ideas based on viewpoint.

U.S. law already contains analogies that show how such obligations can coexist with the First Amendment. The Supreme Court has upheld must-carry rules for cable operators as content-neutral regulations addressing gatekeeper power, and it has allowed states to require private shopping centers to permit pamphleteering without treating that access as compelled ideological endorsement. More recently, litigation over Texas and Florida social-media statutes has not produced a definitive rule but underscores a core point: legislatures can, in principle, impose neutral access obligations on entities that control critical speech infrastructure. A carefully drafted “host-all-legal-content” statute can target carriage rather than editorial speech, preserve space for user-level curation, and avoid commandeering platforms to affirm any message.

Nothing about this approach blesses hateful ideas. It does something more important: it denies any private tribunal the authority to decide which lawful ideas are too dangerous to exist online. That authority is too easily captured by partisan agendas, advertiser preferences, or governmental jawboning. Recent controversies—from pandemic debates to wartime reporting to election discussion—show how subjective rules, opaque enforcement, and back-channel pressure can erase lawful viewpoints at scale. A neutral must-host rule creates a predictable boundary. Government defines illegality through democratically accountable processes; platforms enforce those narrow limits and otherwise stand back.

Critics warn that hosting lawful but vile speech inflicts real harm. That concern is sincere. The answer is to shift power from corporate editors to individual users and communities. Law can require robust user-side controls—block, mute, filter, and subscribe—plus optional third-party “middleware” that ranks or screens content according to user-chosen values. The baseline is carriage, not amplification. Platforms must store and make available all lawful posts; users and middleware decide what rises in their feeds. Defaults can be conservative and safety-oriented, especially for minors, without erasing the underlying speech. Labels and counterspeech tools can accompany contentious content. This “host-and-filter” model protects targets of abuse with user agency and friction while preserving the principle that legality, not corporate taste, determines what may exist online.

Practical administration is feasible. A statute can define covered services by function and scale, focusing on general-purpose platforms that host user expression and exceed a threshold of market power. It can explicitly permit neutral, objective restrictions on malware, automated spam, denial-of-service attacks, and unlawful content categories already recognized by law. It can require rapid, auditable notice-and-appeal procedures for removals, with penalties for wrongful takedowns. It can mandate interoperability and data portability so users can take their networks elsewhere, plus transparency reports detailing any removal or downranking actions. Crucially, the law should forbid viewpoint-based moderation while allowing users to choose their own ranking and filtering tools, breaking the false binary between corporate censorship and a raw firehose.

The common objections miss the structural point. Some argue that platforms are publishers with a First Amendment right to curate. But when a firm intermediates the speech of billions, its function looks less like a newspaper’s editorial page and more like a carrier’s conduit. Newspapers do not hold themselves out to carry all comers; social platforms do. Carriage neutrality in that context protects the speech of users, not the platform’s message. Others say deplatforming reduces the reach of dangerous movements. Perhaps in the short term. In the long term, it drives grievances underground, fuels martyrdom narratives, and normalizes top-down control over contested truths. A free society bets on sunlight, counterspeech, and resilient citizens rather than on centralized silencing.

Internationally, a legality-based regime aligns with human rights law, which protects expression subject to narrow, necessary, and proportionate restrictions set by law. It avoids the whiplash of multinational firms enforcing inconsistent national taboos by defaulting to the most restrictive standard. Instead, each jurisdiction’s clear legal limits would govern removals locally, and platforms would otherwise carry. That clarity reduces arbitrary enforcement and the selective use of “harm” rhetoric to suppress unpopular but lawful dissent.

The status quo is untenable: sprawling, vague “community standards”; inconsistent enforcement; private rules used as proxies for political battles; and a handful of executives acting as ad hoc ministers of truth. A host-all-legal-content mandate, grounded in common carrier obligations and absolute free speech principles, replaces that mess with a bright line. It demotes corporations from speech sovereigns to neutral carriers, elevates user choice over corporate edict, and channels suppression into democratically accountable, narrowly defined prohibitions.

We can condemn hateful ideas without empowering private censors to erase lawful speech. We can protect targets of harassment with strong user tools without criminalizing controversial opinions. And we can preserve a robust marketplace of ideas by insisting that legality, not corporate sensibility, sets the floor. In the digital public square, neutrality is not a luxury. It is the price of freedom. Legislatures should pay it by requiring platforms to host all legal content and by giving every person the tools to decide what they see.

The Digital Commons: Why Lawful Speech Must Be Hosted Under Common Carrier Obligations

In the architecture of the modern public square, social media platforms and online services have assumed the role of de facto town squares, marketplaces of ideas, and essential conduits for civic discourse. Their private ownership, however, has granted them unprecedented power to curate, amplify, and silence speech. This power, exercised without legal constraint, has created a crisis for the principle of free expression. To safeguard the very foundation of democratic dialogue, we must legally require all platforms of a certain scale to host all lawful content, treating them as common carriers bound by an obligation of neutrality. This is not merely a policy preference; it is a necessary evolution of free speech principles for the digital age.

The cornerstone of this argument is absolute free speech absolutism, properly understood. The classical liberal defense of free speech, as articulated by Mill and fortified by the First Amendment, holds that the remedy for harmful speech is not suppression, but more speech. The state’s role is to protect the sphere of expression from both governmental and private tyranny. When a handful of corporations control the primary channels of communication, their private censorship becomes a form of de facto state-like power, chilling dissent and monopolizing the narrative. Permitting platforms to ban "hate groups" or "controversial figures" sets a dangerous precedent: it delegates the authority to define "hate" and "controversy" to unaccountable entities whose primary allegiance is to advertisers and shareholders, not democratic values. The line between moderating "harassment" and silencing "dissent" is perilously thin and historically contingent. Yesterday’s hate group may be tomorrow’s civil rights movement; the state must not empower intermediaries to make such determinations ex cathedra.

This necessity leads directly to the common carrier doctrine. A common carrier—be it a telegraph, telephone, or postal service—is legally obligated to provide service to all comers on a non-discriminatory basis, barring narrowly defined exceptions like illegal activity or threats to safety. The rationale is that these entities hold a monopoly or near-monopoly on an essential facility; to allow them to pick and choose customers would be to grant them arbitrary power over commerce and communication. Social media platforms, particularly those with dominant market share like Meta, Google, and X, are the 21st century’s telegraph and telephone. They are not mere websites; they are the indispensable infrastructure for modern association, journalism, and political organizing. To argue they are "private clubs" is as absurd as claiming a major city’s only bridge is a private club because it is owned by a corporation. Their scale and societal necessity transform their private property into a public trust.

Opponents will raise the First Amendment as a shield for platform autonomy, claiming compelled hosting violates their own free speech rights. This is a profound misunderstanding. The First Amendment restricts government action, not the affirmative obligations we may impose on private entities that function as state actors in all but name. When the government requires a platform to carry speech, it is not compelling expression; it is preventing the platform from engaging in censorship. The state is not telling the platform what to say; it is forbidding it from silencing others. This is analogous to public accommodation laws: a restaurant owner’s right to exclude is curtailed because the restaurant serves a public function. The platform’s "speech" interest is in maintaining a coherent community, but this interest is outweighed by the public’s paramount interest in a free and open information ecosystem.

The practical objection—that this would flood platforms with vile, extremist content—is a feature, not a bug. It misunderstands the purpose of free speech. The goal is not to create a comfortable information environment, but a free one. The answer to abhorrent speech is not to hide it, but to expose it, to debunk it, to outnumber it with better arguments. Sunlight remains the best disinfectant. Furthermore, the current system of opaque, inconsistent, and often biased moderation has failed to create a "safe" space; it has merely driven extremism into encrypted channels and darker corners of the web, where it festers unchallenged. A legally mandated open platform would force society to confront its demons directly, through counter-mobilization and education, rather than outsourcing the dirty work to Silicon Valley panels.

Finally, this framework provides clear, neutral, and administrable rules. The boundary is simple: lawful speech. This excludes true threats, incitement to imminent lawless action, defamation, and obscenity—categories with centuries of legal definition. Everything else—from the vilest racism to the most fervent political conspiracy—must be hosted. Platforms could still use neutral, content-agnostic tools to manage function, such as limiting the reach of accounts that engage in spam or bot-driven amplification, or using algorithms to downrank content based on user disinterest, not viewpoint. The focus is on the prohibition of viewpoint discrimination, not on eliminating all curation.

In conclusion, the digital public square cannot be held hostage to the editorial whims of a technocratic elite. The principles of absolute free speech and common carrier obligations converge on a single, compelling imperative: to ensure that the infrastructure of discourse remains open to all lawful voices. This is the price of a robust democracy—trusting the people, not the platforms, to discern truth from falsehood. To do otherwise is to surrender the digital commons to a new form of private censorship, more pervasive and insidious than any government mandate. The law must act, not to silence, but to guarantee that every voice, no matter how unpopular, has a right to be heard.

The argument for legally mandating that platforms host all legal content—even from groups widely considered hateful or extremist—is rooted in a particular, absolutist interpretation of free speech principles. Here is a breakdown of the supposed benefits and reasons given by proponents of such a mandate, based on principles of unrestricted free speech and opposition to private censorship:

Core Philosophical Underpinnings

  3. State-Action Doctrine and the Public Square: In the United States, the First Amendment only restricts government censorship, not private companies. Proponents of a mandate argue that digital platforms have become the modern "public square" for discourse.   4. Preventing a "Chilling Effect": Knowing that a platform can remove content at will may deter individuals and groups from expressing lawful but unpopular opinions, leading to self-censorship and a homogenization of thought.

Supposed Practical Benefits

  1. Consistency and Predictability: A legal mandate would create a clear, uniform rule: if speech is legal, it cannot be removed. This removes the arbitrary and often inconsistent enforcement of ever-changing "community standards" by platforms.
  2. Protection for Marginalized Voices: Paradoxically, proponents argue this protects minorities and dissidents in the long run. While a hate group might benefit in the short term, the primary historical victims of censorship have been political radicals, civil rights activists, and minority groups challenging the status quo. A strong legal shield for all legal speech protects everyone.
  3. Transparency and Sunlight: Forcing platforms to host all legal content makes the true nature of extremist ideologies visible. This allows researchers, journalists, and the public to study, monitor, and effectively counter them, rather than pushing them into encrypted or hidden channels where they are harder to track and rebut.
  4. Preserving Democratic Deliberation: A core tenet of deliberative democracy is that all voices, no matter how repugnant, have a right to participate in the public conversation. Excluding groups from the platform is seen as a form of disenfranchisement.

The Central Trade-Off and Counterarguments (For Context)

It is impossible to discuss this position without acknowledging its profound costs, which are the primary reasons it is not the law:

  • Platform as Private Property: Opponents argue that the First Amendment exists to protect citizens from the government, not to compel private property owners (like website operators) to use their resources to disseminate messages they find abhorrent. Forcing a platform to host the KKK's website is akin to forcing a newspaper to print its newsletter.
  • Real-World Harm: Legal speech can still incite violence, cause profound psychological harm, and terrorize vulnerable communities. The "marketplace of ideas" is not a neutral or fair arena; it privileges those with resources and power. Allowing hate speech can silence its targets more effectively than any government ban.
  • Platform Integrity and Mission: Platforms have a right to curate their spaces according to their values (e.g., a family-friendly forum, a professional network). A mandate would destroy their ability to maintain a coherent community and brand.
  • Global Inconsistency: What is "legal" varies dramatically by country. A global platform would be forced to host content that is illegal in many jurisdictions (e.g., Holocaust denial in Germany, certain forms of blasphemy in Pakistan), creating massive legal and operational conflicts.

Conclusion

The argument for legally mandating platforms to host all legal content is a coherent, rights-based position that prioritizes a radical, absolutist conception of free speech and a deep distrust of both state and corporate power to regulate expression. Its supposed benefits are procedural fairness, long-term protection for dissent, and the belief that truth emerges from unfettered debate.

However, it is a position that prioritizes abstract principle over concrete harm and fundamentally re-imagines the role of private companies as quasi-public trustees. In practice, no major democracy has adopted such a sweeping mandate, opting instead for a variety of regulatory approaches (like the EU's Digital Services Act) that impose some duties on platforms to assess illegal content while preserving their ability to moderate lawful but harmful material. The debate remains a fundamental clash between free speech maximalism and dignity/harm-reduction models of expression.

The Case for Common Carrier Obligations in the Digital Public Square

Compulsory Hosting of Legal Speech by Online Platforms

Introduction

The most consequential free speech battles of our era are not being fought in legislatures or courtrooms but in the content moderation departments of a handful of private corporations. Facebook, YouTube, X, and Google collectively control the channels through which the vast majority of public discourse now flows. When these companies remove legal speech—including speech that is repugnant, hateful, or offensive—they exercise a power over public discourse that no private entity should possess without democratic accountability. Social media platforms and dominant online services should be legally classified as common carriers or their functional equivalent and required to host all content that is lawful under existing statute. This obligation should extend even to speech from hate groups, not because such speech has merit, but because the alternative—privatized censorship by unaccountable monopolies—poses a far greater threat to democratic self-governance.

I. The Historical Foundation: Common Carriage and the Infrastructure of Speech

The common carrier doctrine is among the oldest principles in Anglo-American law. Its roots extend to medieval English common law, which imposed upon innkeepers, ferrymen, and public warehouses a duty to serve all comers without discrimination. The underlying logic was straightforward: when a business holds itself open to the general public and provides an essential service with limited alternatives, it assumes obligations that ordinary private businesses do not. It becomes, in legal terms, "affected with a public interest."

This principle has been repeatedly adapted as new communication technologies emerged. Telegraph companies in the nineteenth century were subjected to common carrier obligations precisely because they served as the dominant infrastructure for long-distance communication. The Mann-Elkins Act of 1910 explicitly classified telegraph and telephone companies as common carriers. When the telephone became ubiquitous, no one seriously argued that AT&T should be permitted to disconnect customers whose conversations it found distasteful. The Communications Act of 1934 codified this understanding, and the Telecommunications Act of 1996 continued it.

The reasoning behind each extension was consistent: when a service becomes the essential infrastructure through which citizens communicate, the provider's private editorial preferences must yield to the public's interest in open access. The question is not whether social media platforms are identical in every respect to telephone companies—they are not—but whether they perform an analogous function in the contemporary speech ecosystem. The answer is plainly yes.

Facebook has nearly three billion monthly active users. YouTube processes over 500 hours of video uploads per minute. Google controls approximately 90% of the search market. These are not niche services that dissatisfied users can easily replace. They are the infrastructure of modern public discourse. When a platform removes a user or suppresses content, it does not merely deny access to one website; it effectively excludes that speaker from the dominant channels of contemporary communication. The analogy to the telephone network is not perfect, but it is far more apt than the analogy to a newspaper editorial page, which platform companies prefer to invoke.

II. The First Amendment Framework and State Action

Critics of compulsory hosting frequently argue that the First Amendment constrains only government action and that private companies retain their own First Amendment right to editorial discretion. This argument has surface plausibility but collapses under scrutiny when applied to dominant digital platforms.

First, the state action doctrine has never been as rigid as platform advocates suggest. In Marsh v. Alabama (1946), the Supreme Court held that a company-owned town could not prohibit the distribution of religious literature on its streets, even though the town was private property. Justice Black, writing for the majority, reasoned that when private property is used "as the functional equivalent" of a public space, constitutional obligations attach. The question was not formal ownership but functional reality. Today, social media platforms are the functional equivalent of the public square in a way that the company town of Chickasaw, Alabama, never was.

Second, the argument that platforms have their own First Amendment editorial rights proves too much. If Facebook's content moderation decisions constitute protected editorial speech, then so would a telephone company's decision to disconnect callers who express unpopular views, an electric utility's decision to cut power to buildings hosting disfavored organizations, or a bank's decision to close accounts held by controversial speakers. We do not permit these forms of private censorship precisely because we recognize that essential infrastructure providers must remain neutral. The same logic applies with equal force to platforms that serve as the essential infrastructure of digital communication.

Third, even if platforms have some cognizable editorial interest, that interest must be balanced against the First Amendment rights of billions of users who rely on these platforms for speech. The Supreme Court recognized in Packingham v. North Carolina (2017) that social media platforms are "the modern public square" and that access to them is essential for the exercise of First Amendment rights. Justice Kennedy's opinion did not qualify this observation by noting that platform companies could render it meaningless through private content policies. A right of access to the modern public square that exists only at the sufferance of corporate content moderators is no right at all.

Finally, compelling a platform to host legal speech does not compel the platform to speak. No reasonable observer attributes every post on Facebook to Facebook itself. Hosting user-generated content is fundamentally different from composing an editorial, and the compelled-speech doctrine recognized in Miami Herald v. Tornillo (1974) and Wooley v. Maynard (1977) does not apply to entities that function as conduits rather than speakers. The Supreme Court's recent engagement with these questions in Moody v. NetChoice (2024) reflects the Court's recognition that the editorial analogy is at minimum incomplete, and that platforms' hosting functions may well be subject to regulation.

III. The Principled Case for Hosting Repugnant Speech

The strongest objection to compulsory hosting is moral rather than legal: why should platforms be forced to carry speech from hate groups, white supremacists, conspiracy theorists, and other purveyors of vile content? The answer lies in a set of principles that are foundational to liberal democracy and that have been vindicated repeatedly throughout history.

A. The Argument from Distrust of Censors

Every system of content regulation requires someone to draw the line between permissible and impermissible speech. The question is not whether a perfect censor could improve discourse by removing hateful speech while preserving valuable speech. The question is whether the actual institutions that will exercise censorship power can be trusted to do so wisely, consistently, and without bias. History provides a resounding answer: they cannot.

When speech regulation has been entrusted to governments, it has been used to suppress abolitionists, civil rights activists, labor organizers, antiwar protesters, and advocates for LGBT equality. When it has been entrusted to private institutions, the pattern is similar. The Hollywood blacklist, the suppression of information about contraception by communications monopolies, and the systematic silencing of civil rights speech by southern media are not ancient history—they are warnings about the inevitable abuse of censorship power.

Platform content moderation has already confirmed these fears. Major platforms have removed Palestinian journalists documenting human rights abuses, suppressed accurate reporting about the origins of COVID-19, censored discussions of legitimate medical treatments, removed satirical content, and silenced political speech in ways that reflect the biases of their predominantly young, urban, coastal workforces. The moderation of hate speech in particular has disproportionately affected minority communities, whose discussions of their own oppression frequently trigger automated and human moderation systems designed to flag racially charged language.

The fundamental insight of the free speech tradition is not that hateful speech is harmless. It is that no censor can be trusted with the power to decide what speech is too dangerous to be heard. Extending this skepticism to corporate censors is not naïve; it is the application of hard-won historical wisdom to new institutional arrangements.

B. The Argument from Democratic Self-Governance

Democracy requires that citizens be able to encounter, evaluate, and respond to the full range of ideas and arguments circulating in their society—including bad ones. When hate groups are deplatformed, their ideas do not disappear. They migrate to smaller, more insular platforms where they are encountered only by sympathizers, where no one challenges them, and where radicalization occurs without the moderating influence of mainstream exposure and counter-speech.

The available empirical evidence on deplatforming is more ambiguous than advocates suggest. While some studies show reduced reach for deplatformed speakers, others document the migration and radicalization effects described above. More fundamentally, the argument for deplatforming rests on a consequentialist calculation about what speech arrangements produce the best outcomes—a calculation that is inherently uncertain and that varies across contexts, cultures, and historical moments. The argument for open access rests on a structural principle: that the infrastructure of democratic communication should be open to all legal participants, and that the proper response to bad speech is counter-speech, not suppression.

This principle is not merely abstract. It has concrete democratic implications. Citizens cannot hold hateful ideologies accountable if those ideologies are hidden from them. Journalists cannot report on extremist movements if those movements have been pushed into encrypted channels beyond public scrutiny. Researchers cannot study radicalization patterns if the relevant speech has been disappeared. And democratic majorities cannot make informed decisions about what legal restrictions, if any, should be imposed on hate speech if they cannot observe its nature and prevalence firsthand.

C. The Argument from the Rule of Law

In a democratic society, the boundaries of permissible speech should be established through law—through statutes enacted by elected legislatures, subject to constitutional review by independent courts, and applied through procedures that guarantee due process. The existing legal framework already excludes a substantial range of harmful speech: true threats, incitement to imminent lawless action, defamation, fraud, obscenity, and child sexual abuse material, among others. Content that falls within these categories can and should be removed from platforms—not through corporate discretion, but in compliance with legal obligation.

When platforms go beyond legal requirements and remove speech that is lawful but offensive, they substitute corporate judgment for democratic deliberation. They create a shadow regulatory system with no democratic legitimacy, no transparency, no consistency, and no meaningful appeal. Their "community standards" are drafted unilaterally, interpreted by underpaid contract workers operating under impossible time constraints, applied through opaque algorithms, and enforced through processes that afford users none of the procedural protections they would receive from the most minor government agency.

If society believes that certain categories of lawful speech—hate speech, disinformation, conspiracy theories—should be prohibited, the proper mechanism is legislation. Such legislation would be subject to constitutional scrutiny, public debate, democratic amendment, and judicial review. It would apply equally to all speakers and all platforms. It would include definitions, exceptions, and procedural protections. The decision to suppress speech is among the most consequential a society can make, and it should not be outsourced to the terms-of-service agreements of private corporations.

IV. Addressing the Principal Objections

A. "Platforms will become unusable cesspools."

This objection conflates hosting obligations with the prohibition of all curation. A common carrier obligation would require platforms to host all legal content; it would not prohibit platforms from offering users tools to filter, mute, or block content they do not wish to see. Users could choose to filter out hate speech, profanity, or any other category of legal content. The distinction is between the platform deciding what speech exists on the platform and the user deciding what speech they personally encounter. The former is censorship; the latter is individual choice.

Moreover, platforms would retain the ability—and obligation—to remove illegal content: true threats, incitement, CSAM, defamation, and so forth. The legal framework for prohibited speech is well-developed and provides ample tools for removing genuinely dangerous content.

B. "This would violate platforms' property rights and freedom of association."

Common carrier obligations have coexisted with property rights for centuries. Railroads, telephone companies, and electric utilities are all private entities that own their infrastructure. The imposition of nondiscrimination obligations on these entities has never been held to constitute an unconstitutional taking or a violation of freedom of association. The principle is settled: when private property is devoted to public use, it becomes subject to public regulation.

C. "Hate speech causes real harm to marginalized communities."

This is the most serious objection, and it deserves a serious response. Hate speech can indeed cause psychological harm, contribute to hostile social environments, and—in extreme cases—inspire violence. These harms are real and should not be minimized.

But the question is not whether hate speech is harmful. The question is whether corporate content moderation is the right mechanism for addressing that harm—and at what cost. The costs of privatized censorship are substantial: the inconsistent and often discriminatory application of moderation policies, the suppression of legitimate speech that is mislabeled as hateful, the chilling effect on controversial but valuable discourse, the concentration of censorship power in unaccountable hands, and the loss of democratic control over the boundaries of permissible expression.

Moreover, the argument from harm is not self-limiting. If platforms should remove legal speech whenever it causes harm, then virtually no controversial speech is safe—political criticism harms politicians, religious criticism harms believers, economic criticism harms businesses, and social criticism harms cultural groups. The harm principle, without the limiting function of law, devours itself.

The proper response to the harms of hate speech is twofold: enforce existing criminal and civil laws against threats, harassment, incitement, and discrimination with full vigor, and empower individual users and communities to curate their own information environments through blocking, filtering, and counter-speech tools. This approach addresses real harms without surrendering control of the speech environment to corporate censors.

V. The Practical Framework

A workable common carrier regime for dominant platforms would include the following elements:

  1. Threshold criteria: Obligations would attach to platforms exceeding specified thresholds of users or market dominance, ensuring that small platforms and genuinely editorial services are not affected.

  2. Hosting obligation: Covered platforms must host all content that is lawful under applicable federal and state law. They may not remove, suppress, shadow-ban, or algorithmically demote content solely because of the viewpoint expressed.

  3. Illegal content exception: Platforms must remove content that violates existing law—including true threats, incitement to imminent lawless action, CSAM, defamation, copyright infringement, and fraud—upon notice or upon obtaining actual knowledge.

  4. User-side curation tools: Platforms must provide robust tools enabling users to filter, mute, and block content categories and specific accounts according to their own preferences.

  5. Transparency and due process: Any content removal must be accompanied by a specific citation to the legal provision violated, and users must have access to a meaningful appeal process.

  6. Algorithmic neutrality: Platforms may offer chronological feeds and user-controlled recommendation settings but may not use algorithms to systematically suppress legal content based on viewpoint.

This framework preserves user agency, maintains legal compliance, and ensures that the essential infrastructure of public discourse remains open to all lawful speakers.

VI. Conclusion

The question before us is not whether hate speech is good or whether social media platforms would be improved by the presence of more extremist content. The question is who should decide what legal speech the public is permitted to encounter on the dominant communication infrastructure of the twenty-first century—democratic institutions accountable to the public, or a handful of corporate executives accountable to shareholders.

The free speech tradition, at its core, embodies a structural commitment: that the power to suppress expression is too dangerous to be entrusted to any single institution without constraint. This commitment was forged in the struggle against government censorship, but its logic is not limited to state action. When private entities acquire the power to control the infrastructure of public discourse, the threat to free expression is functionally identical, and the structural response should be the same.

Requiring platforms to carry all legal speech—including speech we despise—is not a capitulation to hatred. It is a reaffirmation of the democratic principle that the cure for bad speech is more speech, not enforced silence; that the boundaries of expression should be drawn by law, not corporate fiat; and that the infrastructure of communication in a free society must remain open to all. The common carrier obligation is not a relic of a pre-digital age. It is the legal tradition best suited to ensure that the digital age remains compatible with democratic self-governance.

"The Digital Public Square Must Remain Open"

Ladies and gentlemen,

For most of American history, the answer was clear. The government could not silence legal speech. Not popular speech — all legal speech. The First Amendment was never written to protect ideas everyone already agrees with. It was written precisely for the speech that makes your blood boil, the pamphlet you want to tear up, the speaker you want to shout down.

The New Public Square

Let me be blunt about the world we actually live in.

Three to five corporations now control the infrastructure of human communication. They control where you publish, how you're found, whether your payment is processed, whether your app is distributed, and whether your website resolves to an address at all.

When our founders wrote the First Amendment, the public square was literally a square — a town commons, a printed broadsheet, a soapbox on a corner. Today the public square is digital. And it is privately owned.

Some will say, "They're private companies. They can do what they want." And under current law, that is largely true. But that is not an argument that the current law is right. It is merely a description of the problem I am asking us to fix.

We have faced this before. The telephone company is private. We told it: you may not disconnect callers because you dislike their conversation. The railroad is private. We told it: you carry all legal goods. The power company is private. We told it: you may not cut electricity to a household because of the resident's politics.

We recognized that when private infrastructure becomes essential to public life, the rules must change. That principle did not destroy those industries. It legitimized them.

The internet is the essential infrastructure of the twenty-first century. It is time we treated it accordingly.

The Argument They Want You to Accept

The case for private censorship is always presented as reasonable. Always modest. Always temporary.

"We're just removing the worst of the worst," they say. "Surely you don't support those people."
