If your answer is yes, then I ask you: What happens when your views fall on the wrong side of that line?

And don't tell me it can't happen. It already has. Every major political faction in this country has had legitimate speech suppressed by platforms. Conservatives have been flagged. Progressives have been throttled. Journalists have been suspended. Scientists during a pandemic found their peer-reviewed work removed. Satire has been labeled misinformation. Historical documentation has been called hate speech.

The machinery of suppression does not stay aimed where you point it. It never has, in the entire history of censorship.

"But What About Hate Groups?"

Yes. Let's talk about them directly, because I refuse to be evasive.

Under my proposal, platforms operating as common carriers of legal speech would be required to host content from groups whose ideologies most of us — myself included — find abhorrent. White supremacists. Radical extremists of every stripe. People whose worldview I have spent my life opposing.

Here is why I still defend their access to the digital public square:

First, because legal speech is legal speech. Our legislatures and courts have drawn lines. Incitement to imminent violence is illegal. True threats are illegal. If a group crosses those lines, prosecute them. Use the law. But if their speech remains within the boundaries the law provides, then we are talking about punishing people not for what they do but for what they think. And there is a word for a system that punishes thought. It is not democracy.

Second, because suppression does not work. It has never worked. Driving hateful ideas underground does not kill them. It removes them from the arena where they can be confronted, debated, exposed, and defeated. Sunlight is the disinfectant. Deplatforming is the dark room where grievance festers and radicalization accelerates, away from moderating voices and counter-arguments.

The research on this is far less settled than the censorship advocates want you to believe. Yes, deplatforming reduces the reach of specific accounts on specific metrics. But it also fragments communities into harder-to-monitor spaces, increases in-group solidarity, validates persecution narratives, and makes threat assessment more difficult for law enforcement. We are choosing cosmetic cleanliness over actual safety.

Third, because the definition of "hate group" is not fixed, and the people defining it are not neutral. Today it is a group you despise. Tomorrow it may be a group you belong to. The Southern Poverty Law Center has listed mainstream conservative organizations. Governments around the world label dissident groups as extremists. In China, democracy activists are "destabilizing forces." In Russia, LGBTQ organizations are "extremist." In Turkey, Kurdish cultural groups are "terrorist-affiliated."

You say it can't happen here? It is already happening here — not by government, but by private fiat, which is worse, because at least government censorship can be challenged in court.

The only stable principle is the bright line: legal speech is protected. Period.

The Proposal

What I advocate is straightforward:

Any platform or digital service that holds itself open to the general public and operates at sufficient scale to function as essential communications infrastructure shall be required to carry all lawful content on non-discriminatory terms.

  • Platforms may still offer users robust tools to filter, mute, and block content they personally do not wish to see. Individual choice is not censorship. Corporate deletion is.
  • Platforms may still organize and rank content. They need not promote anything. But they may not suppress legal speech or deny service based on viewpoint.
  • Due process protections would apply to content removal. Users would have the right to appeal, to receive specific explanations, and to seek legal remedy.

This is not radical. This is the common carrier principle that has governed essential services in this country for over a century. We are simply extending it to the infrastructure that matters most in modern life.

I want to close not with law, but with principle.

Freedom of speech is not a policy preference. It is not a tool that we use when convenient and set aside when uncomfortable. It is the foundational commitment of a free society — the idea that truth is best discovered not by authority but by contest, not by suppression but by struggle.

Every generation faces pressure to abandon this commitment. The targets change. The justifications change. The mechanism changes. But the impulse is always the same: "These ideas are too dangerous to be heard."

And the answer must always be the same: No. We will hear them, and we will answer them, and we will defeat them in the open — because that is what free people do.

The alternative — a world where a few corporations quietly erase ideas they find unacceptable — is not safety. It is the illusion of safety, purchased at the price of liberty.

I would rather live in a noisy, contentious, sometimes ugly democracy where every legal voice can speak than in a sanitized, curated, corporate-approved simulation of one.

The digital public square must remain open — not because all speech is good, but because the power to silence is worse.

Thank you.

Absolute free speech, as articulated by thinkers like John Stuart Mill in On Liberty, posits that the only legitimate limit on expression is direct incitement to imminent lawless action—a threshold established in landmark cases such as Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969). In that ruling, the Supreme Court protected Ku Klux Klan speech that was inflammatory but not a clear call to immediate violence, emphasizing that "the constitutional guarantees of free speech and free press do not permit a State to forbid or proscribe advocacy of the use of force or of law violation except where such advocacy is directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action."

Applying this to digital realms, platforms' voluntary censorship of legal hate speech—such as white supremacist rhetoric or anti-Semitic tropes that fall short of true threats—constitutes a dangerous prior restraint. When Facebook or TikTok deplatforms groups like the Proud Boys for "hate speech," they are not merely exercising private discretion; they are suppressing viewpoints that, while repugnant, are protected under law. Absolute free speech demands that all legal expressions, no matter how odious, be aired so that society can confront and refute them. The First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution enshrines the right to free speech, a cornerstone of liberal democracy. While this restriction applies directly to government action, the principle extends to the broader societal need for open discourse. As Justice Louis Brandeis famously wrote in Whitney v. Historically, common carriers—such as telephone companies, postal services, and railroads—were regulated to ensure non-discriminatory service.
